beats.text: It's seventeen sixty-three. You live in London, your love lives in Edinburgh, and the coach takes two weeks.
And it only leaves once a month.
Coaches crawled along muddy roads and stopped every night.
But by eighteen thirty, mail coaches ran day and night, in under two days.
So in seventy years, two weeks shrank to two days.
Then came the railway, the telegraph, and the phone.
Today, your message arrives before you put the phone down.
Their two weeks of waiting are your two seconds.

sources: 1763: one stage coach a month from Edinburgh to London, 12–14 days; about 1830: six or seven coaches a day, about 48 hours. All the Year Round (Dickens' magazine), vol. VI, p. 302. 1829: the North Mail London→Edinburgh in about 43.5 hours. The Spectator, 11 July 1829, 'The North Mail'.
